values.label: End-diastolic volume (LV)
values.where: Chapter 9, p. 119, The Heart as a Pump: 'End-Diastolic Volume, End-Systolic Volume, and Stroke Volume Output' (about 110 to 120 mL)

values.label: Stroke volume
values.where: Chapter 9, p. 119, 'End-Diastolic Volume, End-Systolic Volume, and Stroke Volume Output' (about 70 mL)
values.note: Single typical value; the source gives no range.

values.label: Cardiac output (resting)
values.where: Chapter 20, p. 245, Cardiac Output, Venous Return, and Their Regulation: 'Normal Values for Cardiac Output at Rest and During Activity' (about 5 L/min in the resting adult)
values.note: Single typical value stated by the source in round numbers; it varies with body composition, activity and age.

values.label: Heart rate
values.where: Chapter 9, p. 118, 'Cardiac Cycle': duration of the cycle at a normal heart rate of 72 beats/min

states.label: Intravenous (IV) fluids
states.summary: More circulating fluid can increase filling and, on the rising part of the curve, blood per beat.
states.where: Chapter 4, pp. 160-162, Combining Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves; Effects of Changes in Blood Volume, Figure 4.29A: increased volume raises right atrial pressure; the cardiac function relationship links filling pressure with end-diastolic volume. The same figure shows cardiac output increased at the new intersection, and stroke volume rising with end-diastolic volume is the Frank-Starling relationship of the same chapter; both hold on the rising part of the curve. Filling increase is the isolated model mechanism.

states.label: Diuretics
states.summary: Salt and water removal reduces filling.
states.where: Section 10.5.2, Diuretics: Effects and mechanisms of action: increased excretion of water and sodium reduces plasma and extracellular fluid volume and right and left ventricular filling pressures.

states.label: Positive inotropes
states.summary: Stronger contraction raises blood per beat at the same filling.
states.where: Chapter 4, p. 161, Inotropic Effects, Figure 4.28A: positive inotropic agents increase stroke volume at any right atrial pressure; p. 150, Figure 4.22: increase at a given end-diastolic volume. Figure 4.28A plots cardiac output against right atrial pressure: the curve shifts upward, so cardiac output is increased.

states.label: Beta-blockers
states.summary: Reduced stress-signal stimulation slows the heart and weakens contraction. Slower beats fill for longer, so blood per beat changes little; the flow over a minute falls mainly because there are fewer beats.
states.where: Chapter 4, Cardiac Electrophysiology, p. 142, Box 4.1: beta antagonists slow SA-node firing (heart rate down). Cardiac Muscle, p. 146, Effects of the Autonomic Nervous System on Contractility: beta-1 activation increases contractility; Chapter 2, p. 53, Table 2.2 lists beta antagonists. Figure 4.22, p. 150: negative inotropy lowers stroke volume at fixed end-diastolic volume. Stroke volume is marked variable: a slower rate also lengthens filling, which raises end-diastolic volume and offsets the weaker contraction. That offset is an inference from the Frank-Starling relationship and from the ventricle model of the pressure-volume loop lesson, where stroke volume is unchanged in this state; it is not a quoted finding. Cardiac output down: Guyton and Hall, Chapter 9, 'Control of the Heart by the Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Nerves' (less sympathetic drive lowers heart rate and strength of contraction, reducing cardiac pumping by as much as 30% below normal).

states.label: Venodilators (nitrates)
states.summary: Relaxing veins reduces blood returning to the heart.
states.where: Section 11.3.4, Vasodilators: nitrates act mainly on peripheral veins; vasodilators reduce venous return. The illustrated filling reduction isolates this venous effect.

states.label: Heart failure (weakened contraction)
states.summary: Weaker pumping lowers blood per beat at the same filling.
states.where: Chapter 4, pp. 147-148, Effect of Cardiac Glycosides on Contractility: ventricular failure reduces contractility and prevents normal stroke-volume ejection; p. 150, Figure 4.22: negative inotropy lowers stroke volume at given end-diastolic volume.
